Elder B. W. Saunders, brother of Prof. James and Hugh Saunders, of this county, died in Graves county, January 22d. He was accredited a good citizen and christian man.

We direct the attention of our readers to our advertising columns, which will be found as interesting as any part of the paper. People who read advertisements never fail to secure good bargains.

From all appearances, the chances for an ice famine the coming summer are pretty good. Up to the present time no ice has been gathered here, and the prospect ahead is anything but pleasing to the ice dealers.

The Dyersburg Gazette says that the Garrett Bros, of Hickman, are to locate in that place. The Gazette is slightly off in stating their place of residence, but we know them, and they will prove a valuable acquisition to Dyersburg.

All the "country towns" heard from deny, positively, the existence of small pox in their respective localities, and this would cause one to doubt if it exists to an alarming degree anywhere outside the city of Chicago.

HARNESS, SADDLERY, &C., &C.—For Harness, Saddlery, and all kinds of repair work in that line, call on Thos. J. Kirkpatrick, S. N. White's old stand. He is a first-class workman, and thoroughly reliable.

Every energetic man who embarks in any landable enterprise in our city adds to his own worldly store and increases the prosperity of the city. Let us encourage such men, and, by so doing, we may induce others to branch out.

The cold wave from Manitoba struck this section full blast Saturday. The people of the New England States have had it all to themselves, luxuriating sometimes in a thermometer from 20 to 40 degrees below zero. We are having our winter now.

Mr. Smith, superintendent of the Hickman Rubber Pump factory, has a force at work, and, notwithstanding the unfortunate weather, they have the foundation about ready. A few weeks pretty weather, and they will have their houses under full headway.

City Marshal Barnes shot a colored man, Dick Milner, Monday. The Marshal was attempting to hand-ouff Milner, when he gave show of resistance, and run. Mr. Barnes fired two shots at him, one taking effect in the fleshy part of the leg. The wound is not dangerous.

Hickman elevator and railroad ware- house is "blocked" with corn, awaiting shipment south. The overflow in the Tennesseee bottoms has suspended through trains for more than a week, and it has been impossible to get through cars for any kind of shipments.

"Coasting" was the rare sport enjoyed by hundreds of our citizens early part of this week. The long range of hills and graded streets give the "coasters" long distances, and some nights hundreds of our people, old and young, were out in full enjoyment of the opportunity.
Tuesday week is St. Valentine's day, and we suppose many of the young folks will, as in years past, exchange their little love missives. In ye olden times it was a great day, but latter years it has dropped out of observance. The little daub pictures are sily, but they sometimes serve to amuse, and the young must have amusement.

Spring is heading this way. Soon the buds will begin to swell, the good old granger wake up and drive his team merrily forth to the field, the plow boy loudly whistle, the unreliable prophets predict the failure of the coming peach crop, and we—Lord help us—poor printers, will be bored to death with the usual contributions on "Beautiful Spring."

The present overflow of the Mississippi has caused more loss of property than any for 15 years past. It caught a great many "bottom" people unprepared, and we hear of large lots of corn, horses, mules, cattle, hogs, and fences having been sacrificed in its cold embrace. We can give no estimate of the losses, but in every direction there has been some.

Prof R H. Randall, who has been giving vocal lessons here for two terms, assisted by Prof. C. H. Gabriel, closed his 2nd term of instruction last Monday night, and left for Corinth, Miss. Profs. Randall and Gabriel are thorough musicians, and excellent instructors, and leave their class here in excellent condition, well supplied with books and enthused with energy.

patrick-simpson-kentucky.A1:
A Flight for Life.
MISTAKEN FOR A MURDERER AND THREATENED BY A MOB AFTER HIS DISCHARGE.
HUNTON N. Y. JEANSON L. JANUARY 1805 a
MISTAKEN FOR A MURDERER AND THREATENED BY A MOB AFTER HIS DISCHARGE.

FULTON, N. Y., January 1.—In 1805 a man named Simpson was murdered in Richmond, Ky., by his nephew, named Rogers, who lived in the neighborhood. Rogers escaped, and descriptions of him were sent all over the country. In June last Patrick Simpson, of this village, who went away four years ago, was arrested in Columbus, O., on a charge of being the murderer. The arrest was made on the ground of his resemblance to the pictures and description of Rogers, and it was claimed that he had assumed the murder man's name to aid him in escaping detection. Acquaintances of Rogers came from Richmond and positively identified Simpson as Rogers, and he was taken to Richmond on a requisition from the Governor of Kentucky. A mob of moonshiners, awaiting his arrival, attempted to lynch him, but were prevented. The jail guard was doubled and he was saved from the mob. Three times he was committed on habeas corpus proceedings.—In October, however, he succeeded in showing that he was in Fulton when the crime was committed. The court-house was surrounded by a crowd dissatisfied with the decision of the court. His counsel hurried him into a side-building, and giving him $7, told him to fly from the country or he would lose his life.—Simpson secreted himself till night, then swam the Kentucky river, and reached the mountains. Threading the thickets during the night and lying concealed in the daytime, he put hundreds of miles between himself and Richmond before he dared to travel openly. He has just reached home, worn out with anxiety and suffering.

—A collection of letters written by Voltaire to the private secretary of the Empress Catherine will shortly be published. They were recently discovered hid away in the library of a Russian country house.

—A full-blooded negro was among the Chinamen who lately arrived in Denver; but he wore the clothes, spoke only the language, and had all the ways of his Chinese companions. He had lived twenty-seven years in China, having been captured in youth by pirates.

—The commission on the erection of the palace of the German imperial Parliament was expected to meet in Berlin after the Christmas holidays to consider further details of the scheme. The edifice will take probably ten years to erect, and the work is likely to begin next summer.

—One of the most remarkable incidents in the American trip of Charles Dickens of 1867-68 was his unconquerable resolution to change his American money into gold as soon as he received it, regardless of the rate of exchange, which happened to be so much against him during the early part of the readings that his whim cost him quite £10,000.

—An ordinary Knight of the Garter costs only £100, yet quite ten times that amount is expended when a sovereign is made a companion of that order, and this without counting the cost of the investiture. It is customary to present foreign sovereigns and princes not only with the robes, but with the old disused silver suit, which closely resembles the full dress of a harlequin; the gloves alone cost twenty guineas.

—A San Francisco jury acquitted a prisoner, notwithstanding his guilt was made conclusive by his confession. "Gentlemen," said the Judge, "the mental process by which you have arrived at this conclusion I am totally unable to comprehend; and, gentlemen of the jury, it is not amiss for me to say to you now that the pardoning power is by the Constitution of the United States vested in the President, and it is not exactly proper that a petit jury should usurp that power."

—The Vienna Chess Club, in celebration of its twenty-fifth anniversary, has arranged an international chess tournament at Vienna which will commence on the 10th of May, 1882. Chess players wishing to compete must give notice to the Committee for the International Chess Tournament, Vienna, L., Giselastrasse 6, not later than May 2. The following prizes are offered: First prize, 5,000 francs; second prize, 2,000 francs; third prize, 1,000 francs; fourth prize, 500 francs; fifth prize, 300 francs; and sixth prize, 200 francs.

—The trustees of the late Dean Stanley are preparing, and will present next year a memoir of the deceased Dean. The life of Dean Stanley must include a great part of the history of the Church of England during at least a generation. The letters alone which such a memoir embraces would provide interest sufficient to give it a high place in contemporary literature. Lady Augusta Stanley's letters from the Queen will be especially interesting, and they extend over a period unmarked by any public record of these two lives.

Of Oxford men who attained high political distinction in after life, Sir Robert Peel took a double first—first in classics and mathematics—in 1834; Sir Charles Wood, now Lord Halifax, in 1821; Mr. Gladstone in 1831 and Mr. Cardwell in 1835; Lord Sherbrooke ("Bob Lowe") took, in 1833, a first in classics and a second in mathematics; Lord Selborne, the Lord Chancellor, took a first in classics in 1834; and Lord Klimberley and Mr. Dodson, two members of the present Cabinet, the same in 1847. In 1839 Sir Stafford Northcote, leader of the Conservative party in the House of Commons, got a first in classics and a third in mathematics.

Robbing hen roosts has generally been treated by writers humorously, and a collection ofecdotes on the subject would make a bulky volume; but the Vicksburg Herald, mentioning the case of a thief who confessed to stealing 54 fowls within a month, makes this serious comment: "The above is a specimen of the state of affairs, in respect to chickens and other fowls, that exists in every town and city in the State. The money that is sent to the West every winter from this section to pay for eggs and fowls is no inconsiderable amount, and it is a crying shame that enough of them cannot be raised in this favored climate to supply the needs of the limited population. But the chicken thieves render it impossible."

—The uniformity of toilet which has now become the fashion in London and Paris owes its origin to the Queen of Italy. At a special ball got up for her on her recent visit to Vienna, the young beauties of that graceful capital all wore white in her honor, and she herself was draped entirely in white satin, trimmed with silver gauze, looped with gardenias, and set off by strings of the seed pearl, which is the latest fashionable revival. The white Austrian uniform, too, chimed in appropriately. So in remembrance of the compliment Queen Marguerite, at the first ball on her return, made it known that her fair guests were to imitate the beauties of the Austrian capital. And so at the latest tails in London and Paris the "uniform toilet" is the rage, and ladies are expected to appear in some stated tint.

—The Princess of Wales was once almost as tasteless in dress as her mother-in-law. Even yet her example of screening a neck of rather lengthy proportions has given a ridiculous habit of muffling in England to many of the short and most apoplectic dames. But the visits of this charming lady to Paris have gradually developed a genuine fine taste, and the Princess of Wales is fast becoming as much of a sovereign dictator in dress as Eugenie was. When last in Paris she appeared almost always in black. It is the fashionable color of the moment, and, with the quantity of lace worn, transforms Parisian ladies almost into Castilian dames of the sixteenth century, when Spain was under the severe influence of the gloomy Philip II. The Princess usually wears pearls and cat's-eyes, which the superstitious suppose bring good luck.

Mr. Gladstone, on Dec. 29, completed the 72d year of his age, having been born at Liverpool on the 29th December, 1809. Having been elected to Parliament for Newark on the 13th December, 1832, he has entered upon the fiftieth year of his public life. Of the members of the Cabinet of Earl Grey, then in office, not one survives. Of the 658 members of the first Reformed Parliament, to whom the speech of King William was addressed on the 5th February, 1833, the Prime Minister is the only one who, with a seat in that assembly now, then began his political career. There are in the present House only two representatives who were in the unreformed Parliament—Mr. Christopher Talbot, who has sat continuously for Glamorganshire since 1839, and The O'Gorman Mahon, first elected for Clare in 1839, but whose service has not been unbroken.

The taxable property of Oregon, as per assessment just completed, is $59,-256,275; total tax, $325,908. Multnomah county bears one-fourth of the tax.

Trinity Church of Nevada City has been burglarized and its communion service broken and destroyed. The outrage was committed last Sunday or Monday night.

A man twenty-three years of age, by the name of John Goulden, was killed Tuesday afternoon in the logging camp of his brothers, on Little Truckee river, by a log crushing him.

taire Mill, who was so seriously injured on Sunday last, absolutely refuses to permit his attending physicians to am- pntate his arm, and when told it was s matter of life and death, he stated that he would take the chances.

Vacant houses in Lower Gold Hill, says the Enterprise, are now being sold to persons who pull them down and ship them to Mason Valley. Some are set up in said valley, and in towns along the line of the Carson and Colorado railroad, as dwellings, some as stables and sheds, while others are used in fencing fields and lots.

Thomas Moses, at one time Justice of the Peace in Virginia City, says the Gold Hill News, was compelled to leave Tombstone by "601" the other day. He got into trouble by talking about the Holllday-Earp homicide. He held that the cowboys were murdered. This led to a quarrel with some of the officers connected with the shooting, and Moses carried a shotgun in going to and from his business.

A marriage was to have taken place in Gold Hill, the other evening, says the News, that has been indefinitely postponed. Before the hour arrived for the ceremony to be performed, it was discovered that the bridegroom to be had departed for parts unknown. Inquiry develops the fact that he tried to have his trunk checked at the depot Sunday morning, but not giving a satisfactory reason for his request, the agent refused. Later in the day a ticket was purchased for Reno by a friend, and the trunk was checked. It is supposed the fleeing "lover" got aboard the train on the outskirts of the town. He left a steady job at the Crown Point.

A remarkable use is being made of potatoes. The clean peeled tuber is macerated in a solution of sulphuric acid. The result is dried between sheets of blotting paper, and then pressed, Of this all manner of small articles are made, from combs to collars, and even billiard balls, for which this hard, brilliantiy white material is well fitted.

A poor mechanic from Canada was paid a $50 bill by mistake for a $1 bill by a storekeeper at Granby, Mass. He hastened home, resolved to keep the money; but within a week he returned, gave up all except what he had spent for car fares, and promised to pay up the remainder as soon as he could. His experience with his conscience, he said, had been unpleasant.

Some British ship-owners have begun to man their vessels with negro seamen exclusively, the officers alone being white men. They take them at the same wages as ordinary English or foreign seamen. Those who have tried the experiment state that they find colored men as good sailors as Europeans, and that they are more docile and less inclined to run away.

The Methodist Church at Eagle Bridge, N. Y., is divided on the question of accepting as a gift the money raised by a ball. The pastor has declined the donation, but some of the members argue that, as the church did not promote or countenance the ball, there would be no impropriety in taking the proceeds.

Says the Boston Post: The spectacle of a clergyman mounted on a bicycle, and making a dozen miles an hour, would be enough to convince even the Puritan Fathers that there is such a thing as progress in Massachusetts.

Some of the policemen at Montreal complain that they can't keep their hands warm with woolen gloves, and ask for fur ones.

The procession at the funeral of a Mexican infant which died at Del Rio, Texas, marched to the music of a fiddle and accordion.

It is said that a gold mine has been discovered in Indiana. This is very well, says the Inter-Ocean, but a quinine mine is what they want. SPECIAL LOCALS.

ESCAPE OF ALF GEE.
Full particuiars as related by a gentleman who was in Washington at the time.
Culpable negligence on the part of the Sheriff, if not worse.
Culpable negligence on the part of the Sheriff, if not worse.

When the Galveston News reached here at noon yesterday containing a dispatch from Navasota to the effect that Alf Gee had escaped from the sheriff at Washington many said, "I told you so." From a gentleman who came to this city from Washington yesterday the BANNER learns the following particulars in regard to the escape. Gee was arrested Sunday evening and kept under close guard until Tuesday about 10 or 11 o'clock, when he was turned over to the custody of J. H. Hutchinson sheriff of this county. Mr. Hutchinson it appears paroled Gee, who walked about town by himself, going into several stores and talking to different persons. Between one and half past one o'clock Hutchinson left Gee in company with his attorneys in a vacant room over Dr. F. H. Smith's drug store for the purpose of holding a private consultation prior to the preliminary examination which was set for one o'clock at the magistrates office in another building. The consultation over, the attorneys came down stairs and told H. to go up and get Gee and take him to the courthouse as it was time for the trial to commence. Hutchinson replied, "Gee is all right," but remained in the store without going up stairs. In the meantime the justice and prosecuting attorneys came to the store and told H. to hurry up as they were waiting. It is said that the stairway is inside of the store, which had a front and back door. Gee was seen to come down stairs and go out the back way, but this fact attracted no attention as Gee had been allowed to walk about town by himself; when out, Gee was seen to mount Alexander's horse, which was hitched near by, and ride rapidly in the direction of Hardin White's house, where he boarded; this did not create any alarm either, as it was supposed that he was going after papers or something connected with his trial. He failed to return and after the lapse of fifteen or twenty minutes the people made up their minds that he had escaped, and they were correct; he was gone. The greatest indignation was expressed at sheriff Hutchinson who was called vile names and personally assaulted; he was openly charged by the crowd, which numbered between 125 and 150 men, with having turned Gee loose. Hutchinson mounted a freedman's horse, ostensibly to pursue Gee, but our informant says he was next heard of at Courtney, where he took the train south to Hempstead. Gee rode out of town in an southerly direction toward Mullens' bottom field. A considerable portion of the crowd mounted their horses and started in pursuit of Gee, but after getting a little distance out of town some one suggested that part of them go back to town and capture the sheriff, but when they got back the sheriff was not to be found. A young man of Washington states that while Gee was at liberty on the streets a citizen of that vicinity was seen to give him a pistol. When our informant left Washington papers were being prepared and a petition was being gotten up asking the removal of Hutchinson. Mr. Moeller, the brother of the gentleman who was killed, expressed his intention of prosecuting the sheriff, avowing his belief that he willfully allowed the prisoner to escape. The BANNER has no comments to make, the public can form its own conclusions. We, however, feel satisfied that Hutchinson had nothing, knowingly, to do with the escape of the prisoner and did not connive at it. Mr. Hutchinson,

THE Austin Statesman says that if all the subjects now being called to the attention of the governor are considered at the extra session of the legislature, the thirty days allowed by law will not half suffice.

THE Houston Age has a special contract with Texas Siftings for puffs or complimentary notices. Siftings draws on the Age at the rate of one dollar per line. The Age does not state whether it pays the drafts or not.

ACCORDING to the Houston Post, the proud city of Houston is simply a stuck in the mud community. This is a bad predicament for the railroad center of the great southwest, and the future metropolis and seaport of Texas.

THERE seems to be a general desire on the part of the people and the press that the Prairie View Normal school should be kept up. The colored people of Texas should certainly be supplied with competent school teachers of their own race.

The Austin and Central coal company have struck a third vein of cannel coal, seven and a half feet thick at their Rock-dale mine. With moderate railroad tariffs central and southern Texas should have an abundant supply of cheap coal.

At Temple the citizens are beginning to talk of incorporating. Although the the town is not a year old they want to have all the outward show of a city. The Infant Wonder, a name long applied to Denison, has been appropriated by Temple.

The Navasota Tablet gives full account of the killing of the Moeller, at Washington, by A. Gee and it says: "Hutchinson took no precaution to secure the prisoner; in fact, he was allowed the largest liberty, being unattended by any officer after the sheriff took charge of him.'

Some years ago the death penalty was abolished in Maine, and since then the number of convictions for murder in the first degree has increased to such an alarming extent that there is serious talk of restoring the death penalty as the only means of checking the crime of murder.

JOHN HENRY BROWN, himself an old Texan, has a two column article in the Dallas Sunday Murcury in which he battles manfully in favor of the word "Texian" instead of "Texan." He regards the latter spelling as an innovation. If it is an innovation it has become a very popular one.

NEAR Logansport, Indiana, last Saturday, a tramp who had committed an assault upon a lady at whose house he was given supper, was promptly captured by the neighbors, who made an example of him by hanging him and afterwards casting his body into a bonfire built for the purpose.

Having treated in extenso of Ex-Postmaster General James as "a liar and perjurer," the Washington organ of the Star Routers now devotes a column to him in his capacity as "Sneak Thief." If Mr. James can get a little assistance from the lawyers he will probably levy on that new perfecting press. The criticism of the Critic approach the critical point.

We regret to learn, through the Marshall Herald, that the Jefferson Democrat has been forced to suspend. Col. Loughery says he hopes the suspension will be only temporary; we hope so. The Democrat battled manfully for the interests of Jefferson and certainly deserved a better fate at the hands of the people of that town, who seem to have literally starved it out of existence. There is not a paper published in Texas that can live on subscriptions alone; it is advertising patronage that keeps up the papers and advertising is what the Democrat did not get. It is a sad comment on the business men of Jefferson.

District Court.
Thursday.—State vs. Wiley Holiday, colored, guilty of aggravated assault and battery; guilty and punishment assessed at two years imprisonment in the county jail. It is a mooted question whether—if the sentence is carried out—the prisoner or the tax payers will be the most severely punished.

The grand jury brought in nine indictments, one against sheriff J. H. Hutchinson for negligently permitting A. D. Gee, a prisoner charged with felony to escape and another against J. M. Carlisle, constable of Precinct No. 2, for the same offense in permitting McDermott, a prisoner charged with felony, to escape.

Saturday—State vs. Johnson and Nelson Parker, both colored, indicted jointly for assault with intent to murder. Severance granted, both found guilty of simple assault and fined $25 and costs each.

The grand jury came into court bringing twenty-two new indictments, making in all, sixty-four indictments for the term. The jury was in session twenty days in all. Having no further business before them they were by the court discharged for the term.

State vs. Wiley Holiday; motion for new trial granted. The defendant was, a day or two ago, convicted and sentenced to two years in the county jail.

Monday.—State vs. John Williams, colored, stealing three horses, plead guilty and given seven years in the penitentiary,
He had already been convicted of the same offence, but on appeal the case was reversed.
State vs. John Traylor, assault with intent to murder; not guilty.
State vs. Ed. Bouldin, colored assault with intent to murder; not guilty.
Thursday.—State vs. Enoch Woodward, colored, committing a rape on a colored girl, guilty; twenty-five years in the penitentiary. The parties lived in the neighborhood of Whitman. The case occupied the court all day, the jury rendering their vcrdict after dark.
Wednesday.—State vs. Lewis Babb, colored, murder, verdict guilty of murder in the second degree and assessed his punishment at fifty years in the penitentiary. When the verdict was announced the prisoner who is a stout six-footer, was, apparently, completely overcome with grief, or remorse, or crocodile tears and bull-frog voice, for he began bellowing like a big calf in distress and he kept up his wails and moans, occasionally calling on the Lord, until he was placed in the county jail, it taking too stout men to keep him on his feet. As soon as he was inside of the jail his emotion took a different chute and he uncorked his cursing batteries, swearing at everything in a sort of dilatory and general way. The prisoner is about 30 or 35 years of age and was convicted of the murder of Milton McGown, a negro bay about 20 years of age, near Long Point, in this county in August 1879. He was convicted and his penalty assessed at fifty years in the penitentiary; he appealed and the Appellate court reversed the dicission on the ground of an erroneous charge of the court. His first trial was before Judge Broadus. He then give bail and has been at liberty for nearly two years and no doubt thought that nothing would be done with him.

GENERAL NEWS.
Jas. Shaw shot and killed his wife at Lancaster, Pa.

Daniel Webster's widow died in New York on the 26 ult.

There were 150 boiler explosions in the United States last year.

The river was 16 3/4 inches higher at Cairo than it was in 1867.

Troy, N. Y. is troubled by an apparition of the Virgin Mary.

Hamilton Howe was killed by a falling wall at Strathroy, Ont.

Mrs. Geo. Barrywall shot and killed her husband. at Brooklyn, N. Y.

A negro with the smallpox was shot and his cabin burned at Sunflower Landing, Miss.

Jno. Taylor wife and three children were frozen to death near Lake Winnepeg, on the 7th inst.

At Red Bluff, Ark., a tree blew down upon a buggy occupied by Oscar Davis and wife and killed them both.

Robt Taylor was killed by Dr.
Robt. Taylor was killed by Dr. Sims, a nephew of the famous guerilla, Quantrell, at Perryville, Kan.

Andrew White and W. W. Rea are under death sentence in Tennessee. They will hang April 21 and 28.

At the municipal election at Mobile last week the straight Democratic ticket was elected by a large majority.

Julius Stezloff was accidentally shot while carrying a revolver at Springwells, Mich., and died soon afterwards.

Mrs. Harriett Bell answered the ringing of her bell and a man cut her throat killing her, and then made his escape before she was discovered.

A turkey was confined in a cellar at Clark, Va., for five weeks without food or drink, when discovered it could hardly stand.

Jas. B. Ferguson, a notorious desperado, was killed by Win. Lloyd at Dyersburg, Tenn. It was done in self-defence.

Chas. Sheldon, Harry French and Jno. Redmond, three murderers, were taken from the jail at Santa Fe, N. M., and hung by a mob.

A shooting affray occurred at Arkadelphia, Ark., in which three negroes named Lewis Smith, Aaron Clark, and Ed Clark were shot by two white men named Joe Ross and Bud Henry. The white men escaped.

wm-rice-gwinnett-1882-02.A1:
Georgia Affairs.

George Hester and George Washington, charged with burning a store in DeSoto last week, have been released for lack of evidence.

Three negroes are in jail at Rome, charged with hog stealing.

The residence of Mrs. Whitehead, at Liberty Hall, Harris county, narrowly escaped destruction by fire a few days ago.

The Thomasville Enterprise states that Superintendent R. G. Flemning, Assistant Superintendent F. Predergast, Col. C. D. Owens, and James L. Taylor, General Freight Agent of the Savannah, Florida and Western Railway, were in town Friday morning on their way to Bainbridge. On their return they reported the preliminary survey from Bainbridge to Chattahoochee finished, and that the work of locating the line will proceed as rapidly as possible.

A charter has been obtained and a strong company organized to cut a large ditch on the east side of Chestatee river, North Georgia. Professor Ben Hall has made one or more preliminary surveys and finds the route altogether practicable. Though it will be over twenty miles long and built at a pretty heavy outlay of money, yet it will open up a new gold field and develop some of the richest gold mines in the country when completed. The Chestatee will be diverted from its channel some twelve miles above Dahlonega, and the ditch will pass near the celebrated Loud mine and Captain Ashbury, and then along the divide with the Chestatee on the west and the Wahoo and Yellow creek on the east. It will pass through a gold region in its whole length, but the last ten miles, from Shade Conady's to Martin's ford, is considered the new and rich field.

The County Commissioners of Bibb have resolved to issue no more licenses for the sale of liquor outside the limits of Macon.

Ed. Wilson, a thirteen year old colored boy, of Macon, has been detected in stealing small packages from the Southern Express office in that city. His father has been a porter in the company for thirty years. The boy had stolen about $100 worth of property.

The largest sale of real estate ever held in Macon took place on Tuesday. Several fine stores and building lots were sold, one bringing $50,000, and two others $74,000.

Two distineries were seized in Gilmer county last week by Deputies Witt and Hittzdraw and two thousand gallons of beer destroyed.

Tuesday night, about 8:30 o'clock, two negro men named Monroe Johnson and Dan Grant, both employed at the Central Railroad freight depot, in Macon, got into a difficulty. Johnson made a murderous assault on Grant, inflicting probably fatal cuts in the breast. After the cutting Johnson fled. The fight took place on the wharf near the depot. Officers McCafferty and Wrye went out to the scene, but, after a diligent search, did not succeed in finding Johnson.

The barracks ground in Atlanta was sold on Tuesday to John H. James for $41,030.

Henry Thomas, a young white man from DeKalb county, stepped on a banana peel near the Kimball House, in Atlanta, on Tuesday, fell and broke his leg below the knee.

An East Point man left his horse and buggy standing in front of a store on Mitchell street Atlanta, and on his return found both missing. The police are on the track of the thief.

Two negroes fell out over a game of cards in a McDonough street den in Atlanta on Tuesday and exchanged seven shots. One received an ugly wound in the arm. The other was unhurt.

Jack Morris, colored, was going down a well in a bucket, on Tuesday, in Atlanta. When half way down the windlass broke, and he was knocked senseless by the fall. His injuries are thought to be fatal.

The house of a Mrs. Frances, on Elliott street, Atlanta, was entered in broad daylight on Tuesday and plundered. A quantity of wearing apparel and trinkets were carried off.

It is ruined in Covington and Conyers that the body of Wm. Rice, an alleged revenue informer, was found recently in Gwinnett county, cut nearly in train.

A negro employee of Collins & Co.'s mill, at Gray's landing, on the Altamaha river, was run over on Tuesday and killed by a log train. In attempting to get on the tender of the engine, he fell, and the engine and train, which were backing, passed over him. He lived only a few minutes.

Col. J. D. Rumph, a prominent citizen and lawyer of Jesup, died Wednesday afternoon after a lingering illness of six or eight weeks. He was sent to the Legislature from Wayne county several times prior to the war.

Sunday evening a young white man named Jno Sims came very near being drowned in the river at the foot of Fourteenth (Mill) street, Augusta. He was coming down the river and his boat ran sideways into the tops of s me willow trees that had been very near covered by the high water and was capsized. When Sims arose to the top, after going down twice, the boat was out of his reach. He caught hold of the bushes and held himself above water until help came. When he was taken out he was in a freezing condition.

On Monday a party of guests were sitting around the stove in the office at the Rankin House, Columbus, when suddenly it tumbled over and caused a general stampede. One of the guests was so excited that he fell to the floor, and, without attempting to rise again, rolled him self out on the sidewalk, crying fire at the top of his voice. It was with difficulty that the propietor quieted him in time to prevent a general alarm of fire. The stove was burst by the fall and the floor slightly burned by coals of fire which rolled out.

Berrien County News: "On Monday morning last a difficulty occurred between two negro women at Tifton, in which one of them was stabbed to death. The assailant, it seems, was jealous of her victim, and before the sun had risen went to her house for the purpose of wreaking vengeance in deadly combat. Twice or three times parties interfered and prevented an attack, but it ally sue entered the house of deceased, and then and there, with some sharp instrument, inflicted two mortal wounds, from which she died in a few minutes. The jury of inquest returned a verdict for murder, and the defendant now lies in Nasnville jail awaiting the March term of the Superior Court."

Harris county, who lives about one mile from Whitesville, on the Hamilton road, were aroused from their slumbers to find the dwelling house in flames. The fire, which originated in the stove room, had made such headway when discovered that all efforts to stay its course were futile. Everything was removed from the house, and only the building was burned. «Berrien County News:» "From Rev. Lewis M. Griffin, who came to town on Wednesday, we learn of a most horrible affair which occurred at a party in the Sixth district of Irwin county on Tuesday night last. A party was given at a house in the neighborhood, at which no one lived. The best of order, it seems, did not prevail, and pistol shooting at random was inculped in, as well as the free use of whi-ky, and a difficulty was the result. In the recounter, we are informed, Mr. James Fletcher, Jr., was struck on the head by Mr. James Gibbs with a club, breaking his jawbone and inflicting other injuries, from which he died on the following day at 12 o'clock. He is the son of Jehu Fletcher."
